title: Interpreting slope and intercept in a commercial electricity cost model
scenario_markdown:
A facilities management team analyzes monthly electricity costs ($y$, in dollars) for commercial office buildings as a function of the average monthly outdoor temperature ($x$, in degrees Fahrenheit). The observed temperatures in the sample data ranged from $42^\circ\text{F}$ to $94^\circ\text{F}$. Using ordinary least squares regression, the fitted equation is:

$$\hat{y} = 450 + 38.5 x$$

parameters.objective: Interpret slope in units of y per x and evaluate hazards of intercept extrapolation

assumptions: Linear relationship holds across the observed temperature domain [42 F, 94 F]
Dependent variable y is in dollars; independent variable x is in degrees Fahrenheit

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual question on regression slope and intercept interpretation. Highlights unit-rate interpretation of slope (dollars per degree F) and explains why the intercept is a mathematical baseline that should not be given literal business meaning when x = 0 is far outside the observed data range.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which statement provides the correct managerial interpretation of the slope coefficient $b_1 = 38.5$?

options.text_markdown: For each $1^\circ\text{F}$ increase in average outdoor temperature, the estimated monthly electricity cost increases by $\$38.50$.
For each $\$1.00$ increase in monthly electricity cost, the outdoor temperature increases by $38.5^\circ\text{F}$.
options.hint_markdown: Slope is $\Delta y / \Delta x$: the change in the dependent response variable ($y$, dollars) per unit change in the explanatory predictor ($x$, degrees Fahrenheit).

options.text_markdown: At any given temperature, electricity cost is exactly $\$38.50$ per building.
options.hint_markdown: The slope is a rate of change per unit of $x$, not the total bill.

options.text_markdown: Increasing outdoor temperature by $1^\circ\text{F}$ causes every individual building's bill to rise by exactly $\$38.50$ without exception.
options.hint_markdown: Regression estimates the average (expected) change in $y$, not a deterministic guarantee for every individual observation.

stages.explanation_markdown: The slope $b_1 = 38.5$ represents the estimated change in the mean response variable ($y$, electricity cost in dollars) associated with a 1-unit increase in the predictor ($x$, outdoor temperature in $^\circ\text{F}$). On average, each additional degree Fahrenheit is associated with an estimated $\$38.50$ increase in monthly electric expense.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should facility managers interpret the intercept $b_0 = 450$ in this model?

options.text_markdown: The intercept is the mathematical value $\hat{y} = \$450$ when $x = 0^\circ\text{F}$, but it has no practical business meaning because $0^\circ\text{F}$ is far outside the observed sample range ($42^\circ\text{F}$ to $94^\circ\text{F}$).
The intercept represents the guaranteed fixed baseline utility cost that every building pays even if the building is completely vacant.
options.hint_markdown: Interpreting $b_0$ as a true physical fixed cost is hazardous when $x = 0$ was never observed in the data.

options.text_markdown: The intercept is the average monthly electricity bill across all sampled buildings.
options.hint_markdown: The sample mean $\bar{y}$ is located at $\bar{x}$, whereas the intercept $b_0$ is evaluated at $x = 0$.

options.text_markdown: The intercept represents the standard error of the regression estimate.
options.hint_markdown: The intercept is the constant term $b_0$, not a measure of residual variability $s_e$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The regression intercept $b_0 = 450$ anchors the fitted line at $x = 0^\circ\text{F}$. However, because the observed sample data spans $42^\circ\text{F}$ to $94^\circ\text{F}$, interpreting $\hat{y}$ at $0^\circ\text{F}$ represents extrapolation. In winter, heating systems (often natural gas or heat pumps) have entirely different cost curves. Thus, $b_0$ serves as a mathematical constant to position the line rather than a meaningful prediction at freezing temperatures.
